newsitem.title: UK: Former UK chancellor warns against rate rise.
newsitem.headline: Former UK chancellor warns against rate rise.

text.p: Former British chancellor of the exchequer (finance minister) Kenneth Clarke said on Tuesday an interest rate rise this week would force the pound still higher and threaten Britain's economic recovery.

"I don't think the Bank (of England) is taking enough notice of the exchange rate. The pound has gone up by more than 20 percent in one year. That represents an enormous tightening," Clarke told BBC radio.
He said a half-point interest rate rise on Thursday, taking base rates to seven percent, would be far too tough for the economy.
"But if (the central bank) only raises by a quarter, it will raise expectations that rates will go on rising and the pound will keep on climbing."
The Bank of England's monetary policy committee, newly freed to set monetary policy, will deliver its latest rate decision at midday on Thursday.
"The pound is about to go through three deutschemarks. It will slow down activity, it will have a depressing effect on prices," Clarke said.
Data out earlier on Tuesday, showed underlying inflation rose to 2.7 percent year-on-year in June, just above the government's target of 2.5, first initiated by the previous Conservative government.
Clarke said that vindicated his policy decisions when he sat in the seat now occupied by Chancellor Gordon Brown.
"You cannot be spot on every month and you certainly cannot predict the weather," he said. Seasonal food prices leapt by five percent in June after a month of unusually wet weather.
Britain's former chancellor acknowledged the inflationary threat of more than 30 billion pounds in windfall payments, paid to millions of consumers by building societies converting into banks.
"We do have this one-off effect of building society windfalls. It makes people feel wealthier, it makes them spend more. But that is a one-off effect. Policy should be set two years ahead."
"I would not put up interest rates on Thursday," Clarke said.
